repaired_reference: An SL1 file is the print file for the SL1 printer. A slicer such as PrusaSlicer cuts a 3D model into thin layers and saves each layer as a PNG file. These files and a configuration INI file are stored in a compressed ZIP file, which is automatically renamed to SL1.
original_reference: SL1 files are used for slicing objects for the SL1 3D printer, and they are specifically mentioned in the context as part of the process for printing custom models using software like PrusaSlicer.

repaired_reference: A Raspberry Pi Zero W can be connected to the accessory header of the printer motherboard (EINSY), which provides power and a serial data line for communication. After connecting it, you can run applications like OctoPrint or Repetier Server to control the printer through a web browser interface.
original_reference: To connect a Raspberry Pi Zero W to a 3D printer, refer to section 7.3.3 in the documentation which covers connecting Raspberry Pi Zero W.

repaired_reference: Bearings need regular maintenance. Every couple hundred hours, clean the smooth rods with a paper towel, apply a little of the included lubricant, and move the axis back and forth. If an axis no longer runs smoothly, the bearings can be taken out and greased on the inside.
original_reference: Yes, bearings are part of regular maintenance for 3D printers as mentioned in the FAQ section under 13.1.1 Bearings.

repaired_reference: Polycarbonate (PC) is a technical material with excellent strength, tensile strength, and resistance to high temperatures. It is demanding to print and mainly suits advanced users, although Prusament PC Blend is much easier to print. It is best printed in the Original Prusa Enclosure, needs high nozzle and bed temperatures, and warps strongly on large models.
original_reference: PC, or polycarbonate, is listed as one of the materials covered in the guide, along with PC Blend, under the material guide section. It is included alongside other materials such as PLA, PETG, ASA (ABS), PVB, flexible materials, and PA (Polyamide).

repaired_reference: Z-axis issues include the nozzle hitting the sheet. This is usually related to the assembly kit, because assembled printers coming from the factory are thoroughly tested before they ship.
manual_section: 9.8 Nozzle Hitting the Sheet / Other Z-axis Issues
original_reference: The Z-axis in 3D printing refers to the vertical axis of the printer. Issues related to the Z-axis can include problems such as the nozzle hitting the sheet or other Z-axis issues, which are mentioned in the troubleshooting section of the documentation.

repaired_reference: ABS is very similar to ASA and is best printed in the XL Enclosure. ASA is UV-stable compared to ABS and shrinks slightly less during printing. Compared to PLA, these materials have very high thermal expansion, so larger prints can warp and detach from the bed even with a 100 °C heatbed, and printing produces a noticeable odor.
original_reference: ABS is a material that can be used with the Prusa XL printer. It is listed in the material guide section 6.3 of the documentation, which covers various materials including PLA, PETG, ASA (ABS), PC (polycarbonate), and others.
